item.title: Prices Get Smarter as Deadlines Get Closer — Oct 31, 2026 · 9:40 AM ET
item.description:
Prices Get Smarter as Deadlines Get Closer

Prediction markets are often judged on their worst screenshot: a stale price from a thin market, quoted months early. Kalshi's August 2026 accuracy study measured the whole curve instead, and found its predictions generally became more accurate as events approached, especially in markets with more traders and more trading activity.

An independent check across nine resolved markets in politics, sports and pop culture found the same shape. An 80-cent contract that loses is not automatically a bad forecast; the other outcome carried a real 20% chance, and across many similar markets those chances are the product being sold.

The two levers in the study are the ones traders can actually see before they buy: time to resolution and crowd size. A liquid market near its deadline is a measurement. A thin market far from one is a rumor with a price tag.

Read that way, the industry's growth is itself an accuracy story. Record crowds and record volume do not just make exchanges richer. They make every number on the board harder to fool.

item.title: Same Senate Question, Two Different Answers — Oct 31, 2026 · 9:39 AM ET
item.description:
Same Senate Question, Two Different Answers

Ask two exchanges who wins the Senate and you get two different races. Kalshi prices Democratic Senate control at 71 cents, and its balance-of-power contract puts a Democratic sweep at 70 cents. On Polymarket US, the same Senate question trades at 47%.

A 24-point gap on the cycle's biggest question is not a rounding error. The venues run different books with different crowds: Kalshi's midterm complex counts 311 tradeable contracts and tens of millions in open interest, while the Polymarket US Senate market traded just $77K in the last 24 hours.

Thin books price noisily. A $77K day can be moved by a handful of orders, while Kalshi's price is set by a crowd that has been building positions for months. When two prices disagree this much, the deeper market is usually the one quoting information; the thinner one is quoting whoever showed up today.

Election night will grade both. Until then, the gap itself is the data point: it measures how much of the prediction-market map is deep water and how much is still a puddle.

item.title: The Stanley Cup Market Cannot Pick a Favorite — Oct 31, 2026 · 9:38 AM ET
item.description:
The Stanley Cup Market Cannot Pick a Favorite

Some futures markets have a favorite. The Stanley Cup market has a tie. The Carolina Hurricanes and the Colorado Avalanche both sit at 11% on Kalshi, the lowest leading price of any major title market on the board.

Context makes the tie louder. The basketball favorite is San Antonio at 22%, the football favorite San Francisco at 16%, and even the wide-open college football race has Georgia at 24%. Hockey's co-leaders would be third choice in most other sports.

An 11% leader means the market sees roughly nine live contenders and no separation among them. For traders, that shape is an invitation: longshot prices stay honest deep into the season because no favorite is absorbing the board.

The Cup market will not stay tied forever. Injuries, streaks and the trade deadline will pick a favorite eventually. Until they do, this is the most democratic futures board in sports, and every contender's price is worth watching.

item.description:
The Chasing Pack Is Growing Faster Than the Leaders

Kalshi's 76% share of the last 30 days makes the industry look settled. The growth column tells a different story. Underdog Exchange grew 157% against its prior 30 days, DraftKings Predictions 122%, and Novig 115%, the three fastest rates on the board.

In raw terms the pack is still small: Underdog traded $1.8 billion in 30 days, Novig $3.1 billion and DraftKings Predictions $4.2 billion, against Kalshi's $93.0 billion. But growth compounds, and each of these venues arrived with a distribution weapon the leaders cannot copy: an existing sports audience.

Three newer regulated exchanges, ProphetX, Rothera and Underdog, were only added to the trackers on October 3, so part of the pack's rise is the scoreboard itself getting wider.

Dominance and momentum are different statistics. Right now one exchange owns the first and three challengers own the second, which is what a healthy market race is supposed to look like.

item.description:
Award Shows Gave Prediction Markets Their Receipts

Culture critics used to argue from taste. Increasingly they check a price first, because award season is where prediction markets built their public track record. More than $200 million traded through award contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket around the 2026 Academy Awards, and final prices called the winner in 19 of 24 categories.

The honest footnote matters as much as the headline. Most Oscar categories are effectively settled by guild awards weeks earlier, so calling them is arithmetic more than prophecy. The markets missed in several categories where the argument was genuinely live, which is exactly where an oracle earns its reputation.

Kalshi's own August 2026 research adds the mechanism: its prices generally grew more accurate as events approached, especially in markets with more traders and more activity.

That is the mature version of the claim. A prediction price is a good instrument and an imperfect oracle, sharpest when the crowd is large and the deadline is near. Award season proved both halves of that sentence in public.

Cricket Quietly Became a Top-Five Market Today

American football owns the weekend board, which makes today's fifth-biggest sports market easy to miss: Pakistan versus Sri Lanka traded $417K on Kalshi, with Sri Lanka at 64% and Pakistan at 36%.

Cricket's fit with event contracts is structural. A match runs for hours, momentum swings by the over, and every swing is a chance to enter, exit or reverse a position. Sports that unfold slowly give exchanges something football's three-hour sprint cannot: time for a real market to form.

The match sits on a board otherwise ruled by the Mexico Open, an esports playoff and NFL spreads, cross-sport company that would have been unthinkable in this industry two years ago.

Prediction markets did not just digitize the American sportsbook. They built a single board where a cricket match in one hemisphere trades beside a football spread in another, priced by the same crowd, settling under the same rules.

item.title: Sundays Trade Double Mondays: The Weekend Effect — Oct 31, 2026 · 9:34 AM ET
item.description:
Sundays Trade Double Mondays: The Weekend Effect

Prediction markets keep office hours, just not the ones you would expect. Across the last seven whole weeks, the average Sunday traded $5.2 billion against the average Monday's $2.4 billion. The market's biggest day is the one when its traders are off work.

The busiest single day of the last 60 was Sunday, October 25, at $7.14 billion across venues. Saturdays average $4.6 billion, Fridays $3.2 billion, and the midweek days cluster under $3 billion.

Football is the obvious engine: weekends stack NFL and college slates on top of the always-on crypto windows, and parlays counted outside the category rankings added $243 million in dollars paid in the last 24 hours alone.

The strategic read is simple. Liquidity in this industry is a weekend product. Any exchange planning a launch, a new market or a headline partnership should aim it at Saturday morning, when the crowd is already there.

Commodities fit event contracts naturally. A gold or oil contract is a price with a date on it, the same shape as an election with a cheaper argument attached. Traders who would never open a futures account will buy a contract that asks whether a barrel or an ounce finishes above a line.

The last major North American league without a formal position on prediction markets now has one. item.description:
Bitcoin Fell 4 Percent on the Biggest Hack in History

A $6.3 billion theft at the world's largest exchange knocked bitcoin down about 4 percent. In 2018, a failed attack on the same exchange — one that stole nothing — knocked it down roughly 11 percent. The difference between those two numbers is the story of how this market has changed.

Bitcoin tumbled to a six-week low of $76,368 as the news broke, then pared losses to trade near $77,300 on Friday and about $77,509 on Saturday morning, per Finnhub. Ether fell to $2,178, a two-month low, before recovering toward $2,246. Leveraged traders took the sharpest hit: about $1.5 billion in liquidations, $468 million of it in bitcoin and $358 million in ether, according to Cryptowisser.

Crypto stocks fell harder than crypto. Coinbase closed down 10.6% on October 30, Strategy fell 7.8% and Robinhood 7.2%, per DefiLlama equity data cited by Coinjuice — a reminder that the equity wrappers carry exchange risk even when the networks themselves were never breached.

Analysts split on what comes next. Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan expects bitcoin's price to recover within a week, and TD Cowen, Cantor Fitzgerald and Compass Point all called the selloff a buying opportunity. Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick is the caution, expecting pressure until the frozen assets' status clears. With a crypto market worth about $2.6 trillion and U.S. spot ETFs holding roughly 1.3 million BTC, the shock absorbers are simply bigger than in 2018.

item.title: Half the Loot Is Frozen. The Other Half Cannot Be. — Oct 31, 2026 · 9:15 AM ET
item.description:
Half the Loot Is Frozen. The Other Half Cannot Be.

The fastest number in the Binance story is not the $6.3 billion stolen. It is the roughly $3 billion frozen within hours, as the industry's biggest issuers moved in coordination: Tether froze more than $1.567 billion in USDT, Circle froze more than $800 million in USDC, and Ripple and World Liberty Financial blocked additional tokens, according to CoinDesk.

The catch is structural. Stablecoins can be frozen because an issuer controls them. Bitcoin cannot — there is no issuer to call. Arkham data cited by CoinDesk shows the attacker has already split about $1.4 billion in stolen bitcoin — 18,270 BTC — across 19 wallets, and has borrowed 20,000 wrapped ether, roughly $44 million, through Aave using stolen USDT as collateral.

Freezing is also not the same as recovery. Legal experts told CoinDesk that blocked tokens are stopped, not returned; getting them back to Binance is a separate legal process. The speed of this freeze has raised an uncomfortable question inside the industry: smaller hack victims usually wait on court orders, while the largest exchange in the world got a $3 billion freeze in hours.

That asymmetry is now part of the security debate. The breach entered through a laptop and internal systems, not stolen keys — which means the next round of exchange safeguards will be about endpoints, approvals and withdrawal controls, not just wallet architecture.

Sources: CoinDesk, Arkham

item.title: Twenty Minutes, $6.3 Billion: The State of the Binance Hack — Oct 31, 2026 · 9:13 AM ET
item.description:
Twenty Minutes, $6.3 Billion: The State of the Binance Hack

At about 20:05 UTC on Thursday, October 29, attackers drained an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance's hot wallets across several blockchains. Most of the coins — bitcoin, ether and stablecoins among them — left in a burst that lasted roughly 20 minutes, according to CoinDesk. It is the largest theft in crypto history, more than four times the $1.46 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025.

Binance says the entry point was a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which let the attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal requests through internal systems. The exchange says it later found additional exploit points, but has seen no evidence that any wallet private keys were stolen.

Blockchain analysts moved fast on attribution. TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group with high confidence, citing the speed and sophistication of the operation. The FBI says it is engaged with public and private partners, and the U.S. Secret Service says its investigators are working with Circle and others to trace and freeze the funds.

Two numbers now define the story. Binance has set aside more than $6.34 billion of its own resources to restore customer balances, and industry partners have frozen about $3 billion of the stolen assets. Withdrawals remain paused pending security checks; deposits remain open.

Sources: CoinDesk, CNN, TRM Labs

That gap is the story. Traders still think gold can spike to $4,500. They no longer think it can stay there.

item.title: Twelve Trades for $114.87: Utah Put Kalshi's Founders on the Charge Sheet — Oct 31, 2026 · 5:10 AM ET
item.description:
Twelve Trades for $114.87: Utah Put Kalshi's Founders on the Charge Sheet

The evidence is small. The charges are not. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed a criminal complaint on October 29 naming Kalshi chief executive Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara as defendants, after an undercover agent placed 12 sports trades on the platform for a total of $114.87.

The complaint carries 12 counts of online gaming promotion plus a single count of pattern of unlawful activity. It landed less than two weeks after Utah sued Kalshi in civil court, calling gambling a public nuisance that inflicts substantial harm on state residents. Utah bans gambling outright, and Brown's position is blunt: calling a bet a prediction market, and holding a federal registration, does not put a company above state law.

Kalshi called the filing a crazy overreach and said Utah is clearly playing politics, vowing to stop it in court as it did in Arizona. Arizona was the first state to bring criminal charges against Kalshi earlier this year, and a judge later put that case on hold. The legal map is now fragmented across roughly 20 states, with federal circuit courts split on whether sports event contracts are swaps, while the CFTC has sued at least 10 states to stop them regulating the platforms.

That is what makes Utah different. Civil suits argue about jurisdiction. A felony complaint names people. The timing sharpens the contrast: the charges arrived in the same week Kalshi completed a $1 billion raise at a $40 billion valuation. A market big enough to be worth $40 billion is now big enough for prosecutors to test personally, and legal analyst Daniel Wallach calls Utah a bellwether for how other states approach Kalshi and Polymarket.

item.title: The One-Cent Shelf: $419 Million Traded on Almost Nothing — Oct 31, 2026 · 4:49 AM ET
item.description:
The One-Cent Shelf: $419 Million Traded on Almost Nothing

Look at the top of the prediction-market volume board and the biggest numbers carry the smallest prices. Eight markets priced at exactly 1 cent, the floor, have traded $418,727,767 between them, according to PicksByOdds' live board on October 31. Volume, it turns out, does not require belief.

The leader is "Will Jesus Christ return before 2027?" at 1 cent on $66,761,416 traded. Next is LeBron James winning the 2028 presidential election, also 1 cent, on $54,895,306. Oprah Winfrey winning the 2028 Democratic nomination follows at 1 cent on $54,448,323, and Bernie Sanders winning the same nomination at 1 cent on $52,923,492. Those four alone account for more than $228 million.

The shelf runs deeper. Chelsea Clinton at $51,070,529, Andrew Yang at $48,953,782, Tim Walz at $44,877,007 and Hunter Biden at $44,797,912, each priced at 1 cent for the 2028 Democratic nomination or the presidency, bring the eight-market total past $418 million, none of them moving off the floor.

PicksByOdds notes much of that activity likely reflects traders selling cheap Yes shares to collect small, slow returns, not anyone expecting the outcome. A 1-cent Yes pays a dollar if it happens; the other side collects the near-certain cent, repeated at enormous scale. High volume on a longshot is still a longshot.

That is a tell about this market's maturity. The board's heaviest traffic is not always a forecast. Sometimes it is a yield trade wearing a headline, and the one-cent shelf is where prediction markets quietly became a place to park conviction that nothing will happen.
